messages.subject: Re: model definitions
parts:
Distance-sampling list,

I'm forwarding my reply to Bonnie to the list, with some additional comments
at the end.

Question:

On Mon, 9 Jan 2006 13:35:51 -0500, bonnie hunt wrote:

> >I am using Distance4.1 w/ a relatively simple (but large)10-min
> >point count dataset. Our study areas are arranged into transects and
> >pts. w/ each point in a specific habitat and each bird observation
> >recorded w/ an approximate distance. I want to make some comparisons
> >across areas/habitats/species using distance estimates and have figured
> >out the software for the most part. I have received some advise/done
> >some research and decided an estimate per point is appropriate even
> >though some are using a small sample size to get the estimate...........

> >My question is regarding the model definition. I was hoping to get some
> >advice on what is appropriate for this type of analysis? I've played
> >around w/ the various options and get quite a bit of variance in the
> >density estimates? Should I just go w/ the default? I've found papers
> >where the researchers have used Distance for their analyses, but haven't
> >found specifics on what inputs were used?

> >I'd appreciate any advice.

> >Bonnie Hunt

> >Boise State University, Boise, ID

> >Biology Masters Candidate

Firstly, your specific question about the model definition options. The
Introduction to Distance Sampling book contains detailed discussions of
general analysis strategy (section 2.5), example analysis of simulated point
transect data (starting at 5.2) and real data (8.6 and 8.7). The analysis
strategy is also more-or-less copied in the online manual ("CDS Analysis
Guidelines"), and one very relevant sentence is "We have steered clear of
defining specific 'cookbook' procedures for data analysis and, above all,
recommend that you do not unthinkingly use the Distance defaults."

I agree that we don't have a step-by-step example of the analysis of point
transect data using Distance e.g., in the manual, but hopefully the above
can help you formulate a suitable strategy, along with your other reading. I
get the feeling that there's a lot of grey literature out there that gives
specific advice, so perhaps others could post you information about any of
this they know of and you could summarize back to the list?

Other points that occured to me:

- 10 minute counts will tend to overestimate abundance. See the recent
paper by Buckland in press in Auk ("Point transect surveys for songbirds:
robust methodlogies"), available from http://www.creem.st-
and.ac.uk/stb/songbird.pdf

- A common strategy to look for, e.g., habitat effects on density, is to
predict density by point using Distance and then do a separate regression of
habitat (and other covariates) on density. There are lots of issues here,
for example (i) density estimates are not independent between points due to
fitting a pooled detection function (even if MCDS is used); (ii) how should
each density estiamte be weighted if they differ in the estimation
uncertainty; etc. I think these have been discussed previously - try
searching the list for "spatial model" or "density surface" (possibly also
"bootstrap".

- In your case, with points nested within transects, you may want to
consider a hierarchical model, if you are using the modelling approach
outlined above.

Hope this helps some,

- Len

A couple more things occured to me in reviewing this:

- if you're estimating density by sample (point) then the encounter rate
part of the variance will be assuming that the distribution of counts is
Poisson, since it can't use the usual empirical variance estiamte (formula
3.77 of the Intro book). This is unlikely to be reliable. Whether you're
interested in a reliable estimate of density by point depends on the
ultimate goals of the analysis -- in the two step process outlined above
it's not that important.

- in general, especially if you're using MCDS, I'd recommend using the beta
of Distance 5 rather than Distance 4.1. However, if you're just using the
CDS engine then Distance 4.1 is fine.

Cheers,

- Len
